title: The Weaver and the Seventh Parrot
summary: Kamali has one day to mend a festival hanging. Six parrots are still there. Everyone remembers the seventh, and nobody agrees on its colour. An old weaver, a quiet neighbour and a child with a white scarf help Kamali discover what her loom can leave open.
style: South Asian illustrated folktale in fine ink and mineral watercolour, with woven cobalt borders, marigold, brick red and teal.
coverAlt: Kamali, a young weaver in a teal sari, holds a red and gold textile beside silver-haired Ammu. A ring of woven parrots surrounds the courtyard on a cobalt ground.

pages.alt: Morning light falls across the market and a long blue hanging. Indoors, Kamali and silver-haired Ammu unfold a textile decorated in yellow and cobalt.
pages.transcript:
Once a year, the cloth market hung its oldest story above the street.

This year Ammu laid it in Kamali’s lap. “You have better eyes. Count them.”

pages.alt: A rust-coloured courtyard shows through a bird-shaped opening beside two small woven parrots. Kamali lifts another part of the cloth in front of Ammu.
pages.transcript:
“Six parrots. And a place where somebody has taken a seventh.”

“Taken?” Ammu peered through its wing. “What a tidy thief.”

pages.alt: A patron in a cream coat and saffron turban offers a gold spool. Kamali’s outstretched hand hovers over the spool on the blue cloth.
pages.transcript:
Venu, the fair steward, came with a spool that shone like a little sun.

“Put the seventh back in gold,” he said. “Hang it by tomorrow and the commission is yours.”

pages.alt: Beneath hanging gourds, a woman in green points across her stall. Kamali looks down at the green thread in her basket.
pages.transcript:
“Gold?” Leela stopped stacking gourds. “It was green. I saw the bird from this very stall.”

Kamali borrowed a strand. A customer who had known the bird for sixty years was worth listening to.

pages.alt: A smiling dyer gestures at a length of pink cloth across the courtyard. Kamali holds two shades of pink against the fabric.
pages.transcript:
The dyer caught sight of her basket. “You want the seventh? Hibiscus pink. I washed those curtains myself.”

“The curtains too?” Kamali asked. He laughed. “Everything here ends up pink.”

pages.alt: A potter shows Kamali a small clay cup beside his kiln. The cup nestles among balls of coloured yarn in her basket.
pages.transcript:
At the potter’s, the answer was the colour of a cup fresh from his kiln.

Kamali went home with a basket of good witnesses. None of them agreed.

pages.alt: Kamali lays the indigo textile across a yellow mat in the workshop. A close view shows the turmeric-coloured cloth and the outlined bird.
pages.transcript:
She spread Ammu’s hanging on the turmeric mat. Six birds lay down obediently.

Where the seventh should have been sat a bird so yellow she could almost hear it sing.

pages.alt: Kamali raises the bird opening in front of Ammu’s red sari. Beside the green door Ammu smiles while the young weaver raises the blue hem.
pages.transcript:
“Hold still, Ammu.” Kamali lifted the cloth. The bird went red.

Ammu stepped aside. Green. Kamali looked from the wing to the door. “They all told the truth.”

pages.alt: Kamali meets Venu in a crowded square with the old cloth draped over her arm. A close view shows him placing a brass coin on pale fabric.
pages.transcript:
On the fair steps Venu listened. “Which colour shall we put on the accounts?”

He set down her coin. “I know how to pay for one gold bird. What would I pay for a hole?”

pages.alt: Kamali works on a little golden bird at the loom. In the next panel, the figure remains gold on deep blue while leaves cast shadows across a green curtain.
pages.transcript:
Back at the loom she made him a gold bird. It was quite beautiful.

Ammu passed in a wash of green. The gold bird missed her entirely.

pages.alt: Under the moon Kamali examines the gold bird and the opening in the old cloth. By lamplight she offers Venu his gold back.
pages.transcript:
Kamali held up her two birds. One could be looked at. One could look back.

She returned the gold and the coin. “Will you lend me the space behind the hanging instead?”

pages.alt: Kamali shows the blue hanging to a gray-haired woman holding a white scarf. The woman stands back by a pillar as the neighbours gather.
pages.transcript:
She called first on Nila, who had lived the longest beside the market. “What colour do you remember?”

Nila folded her white scarf very small. “Other people have louder colours. Ask them.”

pages.alt: Ammu, Kamali and the neighbours bring lengths of coloured cloth to the courtyard. Patterned fabric and bowls of yarn form a circle around the empty middle of a mat.
pages.transcript:
The dyer brought pink. Leela brought green. The potter arrived wearing his contribution.

Ammu cleared a space in the middle. “Don’t fill that up just because you can.”

pages.alt: Kamali bends over the blue fabric and works on the rim of the open wing. Ammu examines the finished edge as Kamali holds it towards the daylight.
pages.transcript:
Kamali worked round the opening until the wing could hold its shape on its own.

Ammu ran a finger along the edge. “A whole night’s work,” she said, “to keep a little air.”

pages.alt: The festival hanging stretches across two pillars with the courtyard visible through the seventh bird. Venu gestures to the opening as Kamali and the crowd look on.
pages.transcript:
At the fair the six woven birds faced the crowd. The seventh looked like an empty bit of street.

Venu cleared his throat. “Do we wait for it to turn up?” “Exactly,” said Kamali.

pages.alt: Leaf-green fabric fills the bird window as Leela steps behind it. Next a dyer holds up patterned pink cloth and the bird changes colour again.
pages.transcript:
Leela walked behind the hanging. “There! I told you it was green.”

The dyer went next. The bird flashed pink. Even Leela had to give him that one.

pages.alt: The potter raises a reddish cloth behind the bird as onlookers smile. Venu, in a cream jacket and turban, works his way through the audience.
pages.transcript:
The potter’s bird was red enough to bake a roof tile. He took a bow and nearly lost his apron.

Venu edged forward. For a man who had lent some air, he had brought a great deal of gold.

pages.alt: Venu holds up a golden patterned cloth behind the bird. Later a braided child looks across the nearly empty square at Nila on the steps.
pages.transcript:
When his gold bird took its turn, nobody said it was the wrong one.

At lunchtime the crowd thinned. A child noticed Nila standing where the bird could never see her.

pages.alt: The child and Nila hold opposite ends of a long white scarf. White fabric fills the wing as Kamali watches from beside the hanging.
pages.transcript:
“May I?” the child asked. Nila unfolded her scarf. “If you hold one end. I’ll hold the other.”

The two of them lifted the white scarf. This time nobody called out a colour.

pages.alt: A close view shows two brown hands and their shadows against the pale wing and its gold outlines. From the steps, Kamali and Ammu watch the courtyard in the long evening light.
pages.transcript:
Against the blue there was a little white wing, and across it the shadow of two hands.

That evening Venu paid Kamali for the border. For the bird he left a space in the book.
